editorial:
Imagine losing your brother to an overdose and spending years wondering why the world let it happen. That is where you start with this movie. You follow Doree, a filmmaker who is tired of the shame and labels that come with drug addiction. She starts out just wanting to find out why her brother couldn't get the help he needed, but the journey becomes much more personal. You will travel with her from quiet family rooms to loud music festivals and even into government offices. It feels less like a dry school lesson and more like a raw, honest conversation with a friend who is trying to make sense of a huge tragedy.

What really hits you is the big twist where Doree decides to try drugs herself just to understand the experience. It is a bold move that creates a lot of tension with her family, and it keeps you glued to the screen. The pacing is steady, and the real-life interviews add a lot of weight to the story. If you have a 4K TV, you should definitely stream this in 4K Ultra HD on Prime Video to catch all the detail. You could also rent it on Apple TV for a quick movie night. It is a tough watch, but it is important for anyone who wants to understand addiction without the judgment.
endingExplained: The movie ends with Doree facing her family after her choice to use drugs. Instead of finding a simple answer, she realizes that healing is messy and doesn't happen overnight. The final scenes show her accepting that she cannot bring her brother back, but she can change how people treat those who are still struggling. It wraps up with a feeling of hope, showing that love is more important than being right.
targetAudience: Ideal for anyone who loves powerful true stories about family and mental health.
